posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the compliance pain point as a structural problem with black-box AI, not AI itself, and add the 'explainability is the product' insight without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The ban makes complete sense to me. It's not an AI problem — it's an explainability problem. Any number that can't be traced back to a source and a method is a liability in a regulated environment, and most AI tools weren't built with that audit trail in mind. I wonder how many finance teams are running the same risk right now and just haven't had the regulator conversation yet.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO frustrated with Power BI adoption — validate the pain around trust, not tooling, and add the insight that this is a people/process problem disguised as a tech problem
posts.draft_comment: The trust gap is the bit that always gets underestimated. You can have perfect data and a beautiful dashboard but if your finance lead can't trace a number back to its source in 30 seconds, they'll open Excel every single time — because at least they know where that number came from. The 18 months was probably fine. The missing piece is usually auditability, not design. Did your team ever actually tell you *why* they didn't trust it?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging on dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why dashboards get fat in the first place' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is usually a political problem disguised as a data problem — everyone fought to get their metric on the board, so nobody could take one off. The jump from 10% to 85% usage tells you everything. People don't avoid dashboards because they're lazy, they avoid them because opening it feels like homework. What finally gave you the conviction to cut that ruthlessly?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging on self-service BI failure — validate the 'who owns truth' framing, add the insight that the tooling problem is actually a governance problem in disguise
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so recognisable. Everyone gets access, nobody gets alignment — and then the data team spends half their time explaining why the sales dashboard doesn't match the finance one. The tool was never the problem. It's that 'self-service' quietly skipped the step where someone decides what things actually mean.

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO raising AI hallucination as material risk with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the reframe from accuracy to trust/security, add the 'decision layer' insight without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The reframe from accuracy problem to security problem is the right one. A hallucinated number that never gets acted on is embarrassing. One that makes it into a board deck or a compliance report? That's a different category of exposure entirely. The question I keep coming back to is — who in most orgs is actually responsible for catching that before it lands?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with BI frustration post — validate the real cost of shelfware, add the insight that 'self-service' fails when tools assume data literacy the business doesn't have
posts.draft_comment: That £200k number is painful but honestly the licence cost isn't even the worst part — it's the 18 months of goodwill burned when the business realises they still have to go cap in hand to one person for every report. The 'self-service' label has been doing a lot of heavy lifting for a long time in this industry. Most of these tools were built by people who find data intuitive, for people who don't. I wonder if the real question isn't when vendors will admit it, but whether the buyers will start asking harder questions before they sign.

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market industrial firm calling out data governance chaos — validate the root cause (trust, not tooling) and add the specific human dynamic that makes it so hard to fix
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, three versions of the truth — that's not a data problem, that's a ownership problem. The filters aren't the issue, it's that nobody agreed upfront whose numbers were the official ones. Culture is right, but even culture needs a forcing function. Who in your org actually has the authority to say 'this is the number, full stop'?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing a real adoption failure with enterprise AI — validate the shadow AI insight and reframe the root cause as a prompting/literacy problem, not a tool problem
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number doesn't surprise me — most rollouts assume people know what good questions look like, and they don't. Shadow AI on personal phones is the honest signal here: it's not rebellion, it's people finding the path of least resistance to actually getting answers. The locked-down vs. open tension is real, but I'd argue the deeper issue is that nobody's taught these 500 users what their own data even contains, let alone how to interrogate it. What did the 12% who stuck with it have in common?
